metadata.title: Five Ways to Catch a Resolution Problem
metadata.purpose: Lay out five proposed packages for catching non-4K submissions earlier, with the cost and the limit of each. Explains a proposal; does not advocate for it.
metadata.pair: 1 of 2 — companion reel covers the three workflows these combine into
metadata.note: Content beats are Manim, authored in this reel's own scenes.py, so nothing in the toolkit tree is modified. Bookends use ClaudeComposerAsk, which is already registered with a 916 portrait twin. The outro is a Manim card so the handle is not the hardcoded ClaudeTitleOutro constant.
metadata.reformat: full-length; native portrait graphics; preserve source framing
metadata.channel_title_note: Dropped for the portrait cut. compile.py sizes this caption from frame height and centres it, so at 2160x3840 it renders 883px wide at x 638-1521 and y 3697-3800 - 225px past final_frame_check.BURN_IN_EXCLUDE (x 0-1296) and 49px below the title-safe bottom (3648), which Gate V blocks as edge-bleed. The same caption is 498px wide in landscape and sits inside the mask. The @HumanitariansAI handle is carried by the B10 outro card in both cuts.

beats.narration_text: Fellows build videos with this toolkit and send them to a shared Drive folder. Right now, whether a video came out at four K is discovered by uploading it and looking at it. This is about five ways to find that out earlier.
beats.new_visual_element: The ask, answered — where the resolution question gets asked today

props.command: where does the resolution question get answered?
props.segment: Five Ways to Catch a Resolution Problem
output: readable from the file in about a second
five places it could be answered sooner

beats.narration_text: The capability is there. The toolkit has grown quickly, and the guidance has not caught up everywhere. Four different resolutions are in circulation. Someone can follow one exactly and still produce a half size file.
beats.new_visual_element: Four numbers in circulation — the same question, four answers

beats.narration_text: The five packages sit at three points. Prevent, inside the toolkit, so the wrong file cannot be made. Catch, on the fellow's own machine, before upload. Detect, in the Drive, after it arrives. The further upstream, the fewer people involved when a problem surfaces.
beats.new_visual_element: Prevent, catch, detect — the three positions, with the cost of each

beats.narration_text: One. A starter kit. A block a fellow pastes before they begin, naming the two resolutions, the filename pattern, and the channel. Then one command on the finished folder that prints a green and red checklist. No permissions needed. It will not work on anyone who does not use it.
beats.new_visual_element: Package one — the starter block and the self-check, with its limit

beats.narration_text: Two. Standardise the resolution inside the toolkit. Every instruction states the same two numbers, and the toolkit declines to save a final that is not one of them. It already declines a video carrying placeholder cards, so this is a sibling of an existing rule. It needs sign off, and does nothing for what is already submitted.
beats.new_visual_element: Package two — refuse at the point of writing, alongside the rule that already does this

beats.narration_text: Three. A read only report. A scheduled job reads the submissions folder and writes a spreadsheet: one row per file, grouped by fellow, with the resolution and the reason. It also lists who has not submitted. Bad videos are still made, and they still arrive.
beats.new_visual_element: Package three — one row per file, and the naming dependency underneath it

beats.narration_text: Four. A real versus stretched check. It samples frames and measures how crisp the edges are, separating a genuine four K render from a smaller one stretched to fill the frame. Forty eight built in templates are defined at twelve eighty by seven twenty. It gives a confidence signal, not proof.
beats.new_visual_element: Package four — a small frame stretched into a big one, and what the edges show

beats.narration_text: Five. Sorting. The same checks, but the folder organises itself, and whoever submitted a failing file is told the setting to change. It needs permission to move files, and adds nothing the report did not already have.
beats.new_visual_element: Package five — two folders and a reason, with nothing new learned

beats.narration_text: One thing about the size of this. Packages one, three and four are not three builds. They read the same folder and answer the same questions. Written once, the proposal is two pieces of work and a document.
beats.new_visual_element: Five packages collapsing into two builds and a document

beats.narration_text: Your turn. If you review submissions, the question worth sitting with is which of these five would have caught the last thing you sent back, and whether that check belongs upstream of you rather than with you.
beats.new_visual_element: The handoff question, typed into the composer

props.command: which check would have caught the last one I sent back?
